intro.html: Picture a long table full of good things. Some people take a little and stop; some people take everything in sight. This topic has five words for holding back and five for giving in to pleasure, and they come up often in history and fiction, where writers love to set a careful hero beside a greedy king.

Holding back: temperate (moderate), abstain (choose not to), abstemious (eating and drinking little), ascetic (giving up comforts on purpose), restraint (self-control). Giving in: hedonist (a person who lives for pleasure), sybarite (a lover of luxury), epicurean (devoted to fine food), decadent (soft with too much luxury), voracious (hungry for more).

Two of these words come from names. A sybarite is named for Sybaris, an ancient city famous for luxury, and epicurean comes from Epicurus, a Greek thinker whose name later came to stand for a love of fine food.

words.def: moderate; showing self-control and avoiding extremes
words.ex: Even when the team lost, Coach Ada gave a {temperate} answer instead of an angry one.
words.ctx: Unlike his brother, who ate three desserts and stayed up until dawn, Omar was {temperate} in all things: one slice of pie, a short walk and early to bed.

roots.means: mix in the right measure, moderate

words.etym: From Latin temperatus, past participle of temperare (to keep within limits, to moderate).
words.note: A temperate climate is a mild one, with no extreme heat or cold.

mn.text: Nell’s habits are like a mild spring day, never too hot or too cold: one slice of cake, then “No more, thanks.” She is {temperate}.

scene.alt: A woman politely turns down a second slice of cake while a boy happily eats more.

words.def: to choose not to do or have something
words.ex: Grandpa {abstains} from coffee after lunch so he can sleep at night.
words.ctx: Most of the club voted yes, two voted no, and Felix chose to {abstain}, saying he had not read the plan carefully enough to vote either way.
words.etym: From Latin abstinere, “to hold back”: abs- (away) + tenere (to hold).
words.note: In a vote, to abstain is to choose not to vote at all.

mn.cue: AB + STAIN: stay away from the STAIN
mn.text: At the party, Zoe keeps away from the chocolate fountain so nothing will stain her white dress: she {abstains}.

scene.alt: A girl in a clean white dress holds up her hands and turns down a chocolate cake.

words.def: eating and drinking only a little; sparing
words.ex: The {abstemious} hiker carried only a pear and a bottle of water for the whole day.
words.ctx: At the wedding feast, while other guests went back for thirds, Professor Edwin stayed {abstemious}, taking a single plate of vegetables and a glass of water.

mn.text: At a table piled with food, Professor Edwin eats one stem of celery and calls it lunch: he is {abstemious}.

scene.alt: An old professor holds up a single vegetable beside a table piled high with food.

words.def: giving up comforts and pleasures on purpose; very strict with oneself
words.ex: The runner kept an {ascetic} schedule: early bed, plain food and no days off.
words.ctx: The old sailor’s cabin was {ascetic}: a hard bunk, one blanket, a tin cup and nothing else, though he could easily have afforded more.
words.etym: From Greek asketikos, “hardworking, disciplined,” from askein (to exercise, train).
words.note: An ascetic can also be a person: one who lives this way.

mn.cue: a ROCK for a SEAT: uh-SEAT-ic
mn.text: The hermit on the mountain gave up his soft chair and uses a rock for a seat; he gives up every comfort on purpose. He lives an {ascetic} life.

scene.alt: A man in a plain robe sits calmly on a rock in the desert with only one bowl.

words.def: control over one’s own actions or feelings; holding back
words.ex: It took real {restraint} not to open the presents before Grandma arrived.
words.ctx: The referee showed great {restraint}; though the player yelled at him for a full minute, he answered calmly and simply restarted the game.
words.etym: From restrain, which comes through French from Latin restringere, “to draw back tightly”: re- (back) + stringere (to draw tight).

mn.text: The puppy strains and quivers, but it keeps the cookie balanced on its nose until Kai says “OK!” That is {restraint}.

scene.alt: A puppy holds very still with a cookie on its nose while a boy tells it to wait.

words.def: a person who lives mainly for pleasure
words.ex: On vacation, even sensible Aunt Lin turned into a {hedonist}, napping in the sun and ordering dessert first.
words.ctx: Her brother saved and planned for the future, but she was a {hedonist} who spent every paycheck on concerts, fancy meals and trips the moment it arrived.

mn.text: Sven says he is done with chores forever; from now on it is ice cream, music and naps in the sun. He is a {hedonist}.

scene.alt: A big man in sunglasses lounges on the beach with ice cream and music, his briefcase tossed aside.

words.def: spoiled by too much luxury and pleasure, and slipping downhill
words.ex: The cake was so {decadent} that it had three kinds of chocolate and a layer of fudge.
words.ctx: In its last years the old empire grew {decadent}: its nobles held endless banquets while roads crumbled, soldiers went unpaid and no one guarded the borders.
words.etym: From French décadent, from décadence, from Medieval Latin decadentia: de- (down) + cadere (to fall).
words.note: Today decadent is also used playfully for very rich food: a decadent dessert.

mn.text: The king lounges on his throne eating cake all day while the castle crumbles around him: his court has grown {decadent}.

scene.alt: A king munches cake on his throne while the columns of his castle crumble.

words.def: a person devoted to luxury and comfort
words.ex: A true {sybarite}, Victor would not sit on any chair without a velvet cushion.
words.ctx: Her roommate was a {sybarite} who filled the apartment with silk pillows, scented candles and imported chocolates, so the student’s plain cot looked bare beside it all.
words.etym: From Sybaris, an ancient Greek city in southern Italy whose people were famous for their love of luxury.

mn.cue: SIBBY wants it all just RIGHT
mn.text: Sibby the cat sleeps only on silk pillows and sips cream from a golden bowl; everything must be just right for this little {sybarite}.

scene.alt: A proud cat lounges on a pile of silk pillows beside a golden bowl of cream.

words.def: devoted to fine food and the pleasures of eating
words.ex: Dad planned an {epicurean} birthday dinner with seven small courses.
words.ctx: Tia’s tastes were {epicurean}; she would happily drive an hour to a tiny bakery for bread made with flour ground that morning.
words.etym: Named for Epicurus, an ancient Greek thinker who taught that a calm, pleasant life is the goal; over time his name came to stand for a love of fine food.
words.note: Epicurus himself praised simple pleasures, such as bread and water among friends.

mn.text: Chef Greta cooks an epic seven-course dinner and savors every bite: her tastes are {epicurean}.

scene.alt: A chef happily tastes a grand feast laid out on the table.

words.def: wanting huge amounts of food, or of some activity
words.ex: After swimming all morning, the {voracious} campers ate every pancake in sight.
words.ctx: Sami is a {voracious} reader; he finishes a book every day and still asks the librarian what else he can borrow.
words.etym: From Latin vorax, “greedy for food,” from vorare (to devour).

mn.text: Sami devours a book, then another, then another, and still wants more: he is a {voracious} reader.

scene.alt: A boy reads happily beside tall stacks of books he has already finished.

head: holding back
giving in
rows: ascetic: gives up comforts on purpose
decadent: spoiled by luxury, slipping downhill
voracious: hungry for more and more

after.html: ascetic (uh-SET-ik), giving up comforts, is not aesthetic (es-THET-ik), having to do with beauty. An ascetic room is bare; an aesthetic room is beautiful.

after.name: vo-cloze

opts.s: The hermit’s hut was {ascetic}: a bed of boards, one candle and a single shelf of books.

after.cap: A bare room with no comforts is ascetic.

items.q: The cabin had no rug, no pillow and no heat; its owner chose to live without comforts. The cabin was…
items.why: Ascetic means giving up comforts on purpose. Aesthetic sounds alike but has to do with beauty.

items.q: True or false: an epicurean meal is plain and simple.
items.why: False. Epicurean describes a love of fine food: an epicurean meal is rich and carefully prepared.

items.q: When the club voted on the new logo, Felix neither voted yes nor no. He chose to…
items.why: To abstain is to choose not to do something; in a vote it means not voting either way.

choices: Lila is a voracious reader who finishes three books a week.
The voracious hermit ate only a little rice each day.
The voracious room had a single hard chair.
items.why: Voracious means wanting great amounts of something. A hermit who eats little is abstemious, and a bare room is ascetic.
